title: A robust digital receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution
authors: Lu Fan, Xuesong Xu, Miao Yu, Zhengyu Li, Yunsong Yin, Hao Shi, Xuanyu Guo, Song Yu, Yichen Zhang
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.
summary: This paper addresses the security flaw in digital receivers for CV-QKD caused by image-frequency noise generated during down-conversion. The authors introduce a novel dual-path digital architecture that mathematically and physically cancels this problematic image-frequency component. This results in a robust, high-performance quantum key distribution system validated over 42 km.
main_problem: The digital down-conversion (DDC) algorithm used in continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) lacks rigorous quantum security analysis regarding image-frequency crosstalk.
main_result: The proposed dual-path digital receiver architecture successfully cancels the image-frequency component, achieving a high secret key rate of 11.4 Mbps over 42 km.
method: The authors propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme by performing a non-equal weighted combination of output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain.
model_or_system: The system is a CV-QKD setup employing digital heterodyne detection, where the quantum signal is processed through a DDC stage that introduces an image-frequency component.
key_observables: Secret Key Rate (SKR), excess noise (0.034 shot noise unit), and the cancellation of image-frequency crosstalk.
important_parameters: 42 km fiber length, 11.4 Mbps key rate, and the specific weighting factors used in the dual-path combination.
main_assumptions: The reconstruction relies on the ability to coherently combine digitized I and Q signals to systematically destruct the image-frequency modes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between different detection architectures (Homodyne, Optical, Digital Heterodyne) and the spectral aliasing effect inherent in the DDC process.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the security loophole in DDC, then mathematically models the frequency folding effect, proposes the dual-path reconstruction scheme, and finally validates its performance through practical experiments.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-implementable solution to a fundamental security vulnerability (image-frequency leakage) in a leading quantum communication technology (CV-QKD).
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The three current detection architectures for CV-QKD. (a) Homodyne detection: Signal and local oscillator (LO) at the same frequency are mixed via a beam splitter (BS) to measure a single baseband quadrature (X or P) using one BHD. (b) Optical heterodyne detection: Signal and LO are mixed in a 90◦optical hybrid, simultaneously measuring X and P quadratures via dual BHDs. (c) Digital heterodyne detection: An LO with a frequency offset Ωgenerates an intermediate frequency signal, from which baseband X and P are simultaneously extracted via digital signal processing (DSP).

Fig. 2: (a) Diagram of DDC including down-conversion and filtering. (b) Frequency-domain spectral diagram demonstrat- ing the frequency folding effect. During the digital mixing operation, spectral convolution inevitably aliases the uncon- trolled broadband noise and potential side-channel manipula- tions from the image band directly into the desired baseband, contaminating the target quantum signal.

Fig. 3: (a) The PM model of proposed receiver structure. (b) The EB model of the proposed digital down-conversion with dual-BHDs receiver. Both the I-channel and Q-channel possess image frequency operator, enabling reconstruction to eliminate it. (c) Further simplification of (b), where quantum state no longer contains image frequency operators.

Fig. 4: (a) Experimental setup of the LLO CV-QKD system. IQ modulator, in-phase and quadrature modulator; PMBS, polarization maintaining beam splitter; VOA, variable optical attenuator; PBC, polarization beam combiner; SMF, single- mode fiber; polarization controller. (b) DSP routines. Crucially, the operator reconstruction scheme is applied to correct for hardware imbalances and suppressing image-band leakage after static DSP procedures. AWG, arbitrary waveform generator; ZC, Zadoff-Chu; SRRC, square root-raised cosine; DSO, digital storage oscilloscope; CPR, carrier phase recovery; MIMO, multi-input multi-output.

Fig. 5: (a) Estimated excess noise for eight groups of exper- imental data. The excess noise result of the green sphere is estimated under the 30km channel, with an average value of 0.029 SNU. Excess noise with 42km channel are indicated by red spheres, with the average value underestimated to 0.034 SNU. (b) The secret key rate for 30km and 42km system with the proposed receiver structure. The solid line represents the theoretical simulation curve based on the estimated system parameters. The green and red star is general experimental secret key rate with 22.5Mbps@30km and 11.4Mbps@42km, respectively.
